correctness.rationale: Ghomi's theorem converts each of the three directional curvature-order hypotheses into a reflection plane orthogonal to the prescribed direction. After translating the centroid to the origin, the first two reflections have product equal to a z-axis rotation through twice an angle theta with cos(theta)=3/5. If theta/pi were rational then 2cos(theta)=6/5 would be a rational algebraic integer, impossible, so this rotation has dense powers. Closedness of the body symmetry group supplies all z-axis rotations. The third reflection maps the z-axis to the y-axis, so conjugation supplies all y-axis rotations; z-y-z Euler angles generate SO(3), forcing a ball. For any two prescribed directions, an axis orthogonal to both exists and a nonround spheroid of revolution about it is symmetric in both required reflection planes, giving equality of the endpoint mean curvatures. The bundled checker verifies the exact reflection matrices and axis map.

value.rationale: The focal theorem turns one directional curvature comparison into one symmetry plane, making the natural next finite-data question how many prescribed tests are needed to force full spherical symmetry. The finding answers that question exactly in the first nontrivial ambient dimension: three suffice and two never do. The upper bound is constructive and uses a dense rotation mechanism; the lower bound is universal over all direction pairs and uses a natural family of spheroids. This is a complete, motivated finite rigidity threshold rather than an arbitrary special case or a routine numerical refinement.
